title: En and et — two kinds of noun
goal: Recognize how Danish nouns split into en-words and et-words, use the indefinite article, and name the things around you.
bekal: tell **en**-words from **et**-words and know why the difference decides everything
name what's in a room and the things you carry every day
wave: Go back over **Unit 1** first: cover the Danish column, look at the English translation, and rebuild the whole dialogue from memory. Say it out loud.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Et nyt værelse
dialogs.intro: Budi has just moved into a rented room in Nørrebro. Mette comes to see it.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Sikke et hyggeligt værelse! Er det dyrt?
lines.id: What a cozy room! Is it expensive?
lines.literal: what a cozy room! is it expensive?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nej, det er billigt. Men det er lille.
lines.id: No, it's cheap. But it's small.
lines.literal: no, it is cheap. but it is small.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.id: What have you got in your room?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Der er en seng, et bord og to stole.
lines.id: There's a bed, a table and two chairs.
lines.literal: there is a bed, a table and two chairs.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Og et vindue! Det er vigtigt.
lines.literal: and a window! it is important.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, men jeg har ikke et køleskab.
lines.id: Yes, but I don't have a fridge.
lines.literal: yes, but I have not a fridge.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Der er et fælleskøkken nede i gården.
lines.id: There's a shared kitchen down in the courtyard.
lines.literal: there is a shared-kitchen down in yard-the.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Det er meget almindeligt i København.
lines.literal: it is very common in Copenhagen.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vil du have en kop kaffe?
lines.id: Would you like a cup of coffee?
lines.literal: will you have a cup coffee?

notes: **Sikke** = "what a", for exclamations. *Sikke et værelse!*, *Sikke en dag!* Just like English *what a room!*, the *en* or *et* stays.

**Der er** = "there is". Literally "there is", exactly like English. Don't turn it into *det er* — *det er en seng* means "that is a bed", pointing at a particular thing; *der er en seng* means "there is a bed", saying it exists.

**Adjectives follow the noun's gender.** Notice *dyrt*, *billigt*, *vigtigt*, *almindeligt* — they all end in *-t* because they describe *det*, and *det* is an et-word. If the noun is an en-word, the *t* disappears: *en dyr bil*. The full rule comes in Unit 15; for now just notice the pattern.
**Lille** never changes in the singular — there's no *lillet*. It's one of a handful of rebel adjectives, and its plural is a different word altogether: *små*.
**Vil du have…?** = "would you like…?" — literally "will you have". It's the most common way to offer anything in Denmark, from coffee to a chair.

**Gerne** is a hard-to-translate Danish word used all the time. It means "gladly" or "I'd love to". *Ja tak, gerne* is the most natural way to accept an offer. It comes back in Unit 7 in *jeg vil gerne have…*

**Nede** = "down (there)" as a location. Danish has a pair of words for each direction: *ned* (moving down) and *nede* (being down there). Likewise *op/oppe*, *ud/ude*, *hjem/hjemme*, *ind/inde*. English uses one word for both (*go down* / *be down there*); Danish doesn't.

grammars.title: En-words and et-words
body: Every Danish noun belongs to one of two groups. This isn't about masculine and feminine — modern Danish dropped that split — but two groups simply named after their articles.

Why it matters so much: the choice of *en* or *et* decides the form of the end article, the adjective, the possessive, and the pronoun that replaces the noun. A wrong guess here spreads through the whole sentence.

head: en-word (fælleskøn)
et-word (intetkøn)
rows: en bil, en stol, en kop
et hus, et bord, et barn

after: There's no rule you can really rely on to guess a word's group. There are only weak tendencies: loanwords are often *en* (*en computer*, *en bus*), words for substances and materials are often *et* (*et brød*, *et glas*), and almost all living things are *en* (*en mand*, *en hund*) — with one big exception to memorize: **et barn**, **et menneske**, **et dyr**.

So the only way is to **always learn a noun together with its article**. Throughout this course, the vocabulary column never writes just *bil*; it always writes *en bil*. Do the same in your own notes.
If you're truly stuck and have to guess right now: pick **en**. The odds are three to one.

grammars.title: Der er — saying something exists
body: The frame used to introduce something new into the conversation.

head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: Der er en seng i værelset.
There's a bed in the room.
Der er mange cykler i København.
There are many bikes in Copenhagen.

after: Notice the question is made by swapping *er* and *der*, with no helper word at all. Danish has no equivalent of English *do* — questions are made purely by moving the verb to the front. We'll see this again and again.

blocks.text: Learn each line **with its en or et**. Learning just *bord* is useless; what's useful is *et bord*.

blocks.title: Memory tricks that actually work
items: Write nouns in your notes **in different colors** for en-words and et-words. The brain remembers colors far better than the label "fælleskøn".
Or: don't learn the word, learn a **short sentence** containing it. *Jeg har et bord* sticks better than "bord = table (et)".
Don't learn two contrasting words side by side (*en stol* / *et bord*) in the same session — the brain mixes them up. Space them out.

blocks.text: The easy part of the Danish number system. The hard part waits in Unit 6.

⚠️ The number **1** has two forms, chosen by the noun's group — exactly like the article: *en bil* (one car), *et hus* (one house). That's no coincidence; the articles *en/et* come from the number one. From two upward, there's no difference.
*Seksten* is pronounced **SAIS-tuhn**, not "sex-ten" — the *k* is silent. It's the number beginners misread most often.

items: There's a table in the room.
The room is small but cheap.
Would you like a cup of coffee?
There are two chairs and one window.

exercises.prompt: Choose der er or det er.
Put the words in the right order.
items: kaffe / have / du / vil / en / kop / ?
stole / og / en / to / seng / er / der

answers: et — en — et — en — et — en — et — en
Der er et bord i værelset. — Jeg har ikke et køleskab. — Er der et køkken? — Værelset er lille, men billigt. — Vil du have en kop kaffe? — Der er to stole og et vindue.
Der er — Det er — Der er — Det er — Der er
Der er et vindue. — Jeg har ikke et køleskab. — Værelset er billigt. — Vil du have en kop kaffe? — Der er en seng og to stole.
